Journal of risk and financial management

The aim of our paper is to construct a multidimensional financial inclusion (FI) index to measure the level of FI in 91 countries across different income groups. In order to address our research problem, we use the principal component analysis method. This approach addresses the criticism of the arbitrary selection of weights and reflects the degree of financial inclusion in depth. The data are drawn from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Financial Access Survey (FAS), the World Development Indicators (World Bank) and the Global Findex Database during the period of 2004–2020. This paper is the first to consider so many indicators of financial inclusion (13 indicators), belonging to three different dimensions of FI, in order to take into account the maximum number of aspects related to this concept. In addition, unlike previous work, this paper considers both developing and developed countries, which makes it possible to identify differences between them. The proposed index has some advantages. First, it is robust, comparable across countries and has good predictive power in tracking household microeconomic indicators (accounts and savings). It is also well correlated with macroeconomic variables such as literacy rate, poverty, GINI index, real interest rate and employers. Second, our results clearly show that, as a country’s income level grows higher, its level of financial inclusion also grows higher.

data.Documented value: The unintended impact of housing provident fund on income inequality in urban China

We use the China Household Income Project (CHIP) data to evaluate the impact of the Housing Provident Fund (HPF) on income inequality in urban China. We find that urban residents differ significantly in their accessibility to and intensity of utilization of the HPF. Those who work in the public sector, in monopolistic industries, and possess managerial or professional occupations are more likely to benefit from the HPF, leading to further income inequality. Our research also emphasizes four mechanisms through which the HPF affects income inequality. The foregone interest due to compulsory HPF saving is the only mechanism that decreases the inequality, whereas the employer's match, personal income tax exemption on the HPF, and lower interest expense due to acquiring the HPF loan increase inequality. The evidence highlights the HPF's unintended redistributive impacts and thus the necessity of enhancing equity in the ongoing HPF reform.

sections.heading: Developing a Multidimensional Financial Inclusion Index: A Comparison Based on
paragraphs: ### Developing a Multidimensional Financial Inclusion Index: A Comparison Based on Income Groups [[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]] In the realm of financial inclusion, the concept of multidimensional financial inclusion (FI) is crucial for understanding how different groups within a country's population access and utilize financial services. This paper aims to construct a multidimensional FI index to measure the level of FI across 91 countries, considering various income groups. The principal component analysis method is employed to address the criticism of arbitrary weight selection and to provide a deeper reflection of financial inclusion. The data used comes from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Financial Access Survey (FAS), the World Development Indicators (World Bank), and the Global Findex Database, covering the period from 2004 to 2020.

[[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]] The paper's approach is innovative in that it considers 13 indicators across three dimensions of FI: access to financial services, financial literacy, and financial awareness. Unlike previous work, this study considers both developing and developed countries, providing a comprehensive comparison. The proposed index has several advantages. Firstly, it is robust, comparable across countries, and has good predictive power in tracking household microeconomic indicators, such as accounts and savings.

Additionally, it is well correlated with macroeconomic variables like literacy rate, poverty, GINI index, real interest rate, and employers. Secondly, the results clearly show that as a country's income level grows higher, its level of financial inclusion also grows higher. [[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]] ### Sustainability: Who Benefits from the Housing Provident Fund System in China? [[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]] The Housing Provident Fund System (HPFS) was established in China in the 1990s as a welfare program to offer low-cost loans and encourage the purchase of houses.

However, there has been controversy over the income redistribution effect of HPFS. Previous studies focused on the effect of low-interest-rate loans but ignored the effects of tax exemptions and low-interest-rate deposits. This paper introduces a lifetime cash flow model that considers these effects together. It compares the internal rate of return (IRR) for typical employees with different incomes in four situations: whether or not HPFS participation and whether or not house purchasing. [[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]]

The findings reveal that the IRRs of typical low-income HPFS participants who buy houses with HPFS loans are lower than those of non-participants who buy houses with commercial mortgages without HPFS participation. For middle-income employees, there is not much difference in IRR between the two situations. Only high-income employees can benefit from HPFS participation, primarily due to the tax exemptions, rather than the effect of low-interest-rate loans. Increasing the coverage of HPFS and HPFS loans among low-income employees will not improve the income redistribution effect of HPFS. [[S1|Journal of risk and financial management]]

sections.heading: The unintended impact of housing provident fund on income inequality
paragraphs: **How Can I Declare My Interest Income on Provident Fund?** [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] In the context of urban China, the Housing Provident Fund (HPF) has become a significant financial tool for many residents, aiming to provide a safety net for housing costs. However, the impact of this fund on income inequality is not always straightforward. This article explores how the HPF can inadvertently exacerbate income disparities, particularly among urban residents. [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] The China Household Income Project (CHIP) data reveals that urban residents exhibit significant differences in their access to and utilization of the HPF.

Individuals working in the public sector, in monopolistic industries, or those with managerial or professional occupations are more likely to benefit from the HPF. This disparity in access and utilization leads to further income inequality. The research emphasizes four mechanisms through which the HPF affects income inequality: [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] 1. **Foregone Interest Due to Compulsory HPF Saving**: The HPF is a compulsory savings scheme, and individuals who participate in it forego the interest they could have earned on their savings.

This foregone interest is the only mechanism that decreases income inequality. Conversely, the employer's match, personal income tax exemption on the HPF, and lower interest expense due to acquiring the HPF loan increase income inequality. [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] 2. **Employer's Match**: The employer's contribution to the HPF can lead to a reduction in the individual's disposable income, thereby increasing income inequality.

[[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] **Personal Income Tax Exemption on HPF**: While the HPF provides a tax exemption, the individual still pays income tax on the amount contributed to the HPF. This tax burden can be significant, leading to a decrease in disposable income and further income inequality. [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] **Lower Interest Expense Due to Acquiring the HPF Loan**: The interest expense on the HPF loan is lower compared to the interest earned on the HPF savings, leading to a decrease in disposable income and income inequality. [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] The evidence highlights the HPF's unintended redistributive impacts, emphasizing the necessity of enhancing equity in the ongoing HPF reform.

This reform should consider the mechanisms that contribute to income inequality and address them through targeted interventions. [[S3|China Economic Quarterly International]] In conclusion, while the HPF is intended to provide a safety net for housing costs, it can inadvertently exacerbate income inequality.

[[S5|ResearchSpace University of KwaZulu-Natal]] When it comes to declaring interest income on your provident fund, it's important to understand the process and ensure you're doing it correctly. The Rennies Provident Fund, for instance, has been under scrutiny for its investment management strategy. This study, conducted by the University of KwaZulu-Natal, aimed to determine whether the fund's management strategy created or destroyed shareholder value over a 17-year period.

[[S5|ResearchSpace University of KwaZulu-Natal]] The study reviewed the Rennies Provident Fund's performance against its internally set performance objective of returning the Consumer Price Index (CPI) plus 3%. It also compared the fund's performance to that of similar pension funds over a 12-year period. The findings revealed that while the fund has generally met its internal benchmark, it performed poorly when compared to other similar funds. This suggests that the fund's management strategy may not be as effective as expected.

[[S5|ResearchSpace University of KwaZulu-Natal]] The value-based performance measurement approach applied to the fund found that shareholder value was destroyed in absolute money terms over the 17-year review period. This indicates that the fund's investment strategy may not be achieving the desired financial outcomes for its members. paragraphs: ### How can I declare my interest income on provid [[S2|Agronomy]] Interest income from provident funds is typically declared on a quarterly basis, usually in April, July, October, and January. This is because the interest earned is based on the balance of your account at the end of each quarter, and the interest is credited to your account on the last day of the quarter. [[S2|Agronomy]] To declare your interest income, you need to provide the following information: [[S2|Agronomy]] **Account Number**: Your provident fund account number is usually provided by the provident fund organization. 2.

**Interest Amount**: The interest earned during the quarter. **Quarterly Statement**: A statement that shows the balance of your account at the end of each quarter. **Declaration Form**: A form that you need to fill out to declare your interest income. This form is usually available on the website of the provident fund organization or through the organization’s customer service center.

[[S2|Agronomy]] [[S2|Agronomy]] Once you have all the necessary information, you can submit your declaration form. The process is usually straightforward, and you can usually do it online, by phone, or in person at the organization’s office. [[S2|Agronomy]] ### Does the Level of Financial Cognition Affect the Income of Rural Households? [[S2|Agronomy]] The level of financial cognition, or the ability to understand and use financial information effectively, can significantly impact the income of rural households.

This is evident from the study "Agronomy: Does the Level of Financial Cognition Affect the Income of Rural Households?" which found that financial cognitive ability is an important part of human capital, which has a direct impact on household income. [[S2|Agronomy]] The dual differences composed by rural residents' cognition level and residents' income make the relationship between the two complicated. This means that the impact of financial cognition on household income can vary depending on the individual's financial literacy and the income level of the household. For instance, a household with higher financial cognition might be able to make better use of financial information to increase its income, while a household with lower financial cognition might struggle to understand and use financial information effectively.

[[S2|Agronomy]] This study also takes into account the individual heterogeneity of financial cognition, which means that the impact of financial cognition on household income can vary from person to person.
